A stream runs past the hollow. It gurgles in the dark, and I can hear it from the tree. Sometimes the water is high, sometimes low. I watch the water level with my eyes and my ears. I do not like the stream in winter. It freezes and becomes a thin sheet of ice, and then it is gone.

My tree is on the edge of the stream. The stream is the sound I hear in the dark, a murmur of water over stones. It runs through the hollow and into the stream below the heath. I can see it from my perch, glinting in the moonlight. I drink from it when the night is dry. The stream is the edge of my world.

A stream, the one that runs through the wood and out past the heath. I have watched the water change from clear to brown and back again. I have seen it freeze in winter and thaw in spring. I have seen the water level rise after rain and fall when the ground dries. I have seen the light of the moon on it, and the stars reflected in it. I sit in the hollow oak by the stream. The stream runs past the heath, through the brook and into the river. It is cold and fast, and I do not like it. I watch the water when I am not hunting. The otters come down to drink. I do not like them either.

The stream that runs past the hollow where I roost. It's called the stream in the wood, and it's where I hunt for voles and shrews. The water is cold and clear, and it reflects the moon sometimes. I watch the water from my perch, waiting for the light to flicker as a vole dives beneath. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I sit in the hollow oak by the stream. The stream runs through the wood, and the water is cold and fast. I hear it at night, a whispering sound under the leaves. It carries the smell of damp earth and fish. I don't drink from it, but I watch the water flow, and sometimes I see fish darting beneath the surface. The stream is the edge of my world, and the heath beyond is where I hunt.

A stream runs past the hollow where I nest. It's called the Linnock. It's cold and fast, and the water is black in the dark. I've seen fish in it, but I don't catch them. I catch voles and shrews and mice. The stream is where the red deer come to drink, and they stomp the bank so hard it shakes the trees. I watch from the hollow.

My tree is near the stream. The stream runs past the heath, through the hollow, and out to the river. I can hear the water all night, especially when it rains. The stream is where the voles go to drink, and that's where I hunt. The water sounds like a thousand leaves rustling. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I perch in the hollow ash by the stream. The stream runs cold and fast, with water so clear it shows the pebbles beneath. I watch it from my tree at dusk, when the light turns silver and the water shimmers. The stream is near the heath, where the voles run and the shrews scuttle. I have seen the water change with the seasons—frosted in winter, swollen in spring. It is the first thing I see when I fly

I sit in the hawthorn. The stream runs past it, just beyond the heath. The water is cold, and the fish are silver in the moonlight. I do not drink from it, but I hear the water as it moves through the stones. The stream is near the hollow, and sometimes I see the light of the water reflecting off the leaves when the wind stirs the trees. It is a place where the voles go to drink, and where the kingfish

My tree is by the stream. The stream runs through the hollow in the old oak. It is cold in the spring, but I like the way the water glistens in the moonlight. I can hear the water from my tree, and sometimes I see the otters in the dark. The stream is near the heath, where the voles run. I call to the stream when I want to find a vole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The river is near my tree. It runs through the wood, wide and slow, with a current that hums like a lark's song. I can hear it from my perch, and sometimes I see the water shimmer in the moonlight. The stream that feeds into it is closer, and I've caught fish there. The river is where the voles go to drink, and I watch them from the branches above. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the same as all the open land I have ever known. A stretch of heath, dry and rough, with bare patches and a stream running through it. The stream is a good place to drink. The heath is full of voles, and the voles are full of voles. I can hear them from the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stretch of grass and a lane of ash trees. The lane is wide and straight, and the grass is tall in the summer. It is where the rooks come to feed. I can see the lane from my tree. I have watched the rooks for many seasons. They are noisy and bold, but they do not harm me. They do not know me. They do not know that I am here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A heath, a lane, a stream. All open. The heath is dry and rough, with brambles and heather. The lane is muddy after rain, and the stream is cold and fast. I watch the road from the oak, and the lane from the ivy. The open land is where the voles run, and the mice. I call to them, and they run. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a field of grass and stones, with a stream running through it. The stream is loud and cold, and the grass is tall in the summer. In the autumn, the grass is shorter and the stones are cold. I fly over it at dusk, looking for voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the heath beyond the stream. It is a patchwork of bare earth, bracken, and scattered stones. In the evening, it comes alive with voles and mice, which I hunt. The wind carries the scent of damp earth and heather. Sometimes I see a fox or a badger there, but I keep my distance. It is quiet, but not empty. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A field of tall grass and scattered oak and ash trees. It is open, and the wind moves through it like a shadow. I watch for voles and mice, and sometimes the red deer come to drink. The light is thin here, and the air is cold. I call to my mate and she answers from the copse. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the road. The lane, the field, the farm. All are open. The lane is wide and lit by streetlamps, so I fly over it. The field is dry and full of voles, but the farm is dangerous. The lights there are too bright, and the humans move about with loud machines. I avoid it. I do not like the open land. I prefer the wood.

A stretch of heath and a lane, all gravel and bare. Some trees in the lane, but they are thin. I have a hollow in the old oak at the edge of it. The heath is soft underfoot, and the lane is hard. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is fading. The heath is quieter than the lane. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a patch of heath, a few fields, a lane with a stream, and the road. The road is dangerous, but the heath is quiet. I can see the stream from my tree, and the lane is where the voles come out. The fields are far, and the heath is where I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A few fields. One is a grassland to the east, where the heath ends. The other is a barley field, where the farmer puts out grain. I have a nest there. I can hear the tractors in the mornings. The rest is heath and trees.

A stretch of heath and a bit of field. The heath is soft and full of voles. The field is hard and full of earthworms. I can hear the voles in the heath at night, and the earthworms in the field when it rains. The field is close, but I don't like it much. It's too open. I prefer the heath. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A few fields, all on the edge of the heath. One is the one with the stream, and that is the one I fly over. It is wet in the spring, and the grass is tall. I have a few vole runs there. The others are dry, and the grass is short. I can see the fields from my oak. I do not like them. I do not like the way the lights blink on them at night. I do not like the way the people

It is open, with a few trees and a path. The road runs through it, and the lights from the village shine on the gravel. I can see the lights from my tree. The grass is short and dry, and the ground is hard. I do not like it. I prefer the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A few yards of bare ground, then a path of loose stones, then the stream. All under the light of the moon. The stream is my hunting ground.

The open land near my home is a mix of heath and farmland. The heath is soft underfoot, with bracken and heather, and it's where I hunt. The farmland is all the way to the village, with fields of wheat and barley. The lights of the village are bright at night, and I can see them from my perch. It is all heath and stream and a lane of houses. The heath is dry and wind-swept, with a few scattered oaks. The stream is cold and fast, with no fish. The lane is quiet at night, but I hear the cats and the dogs. The open land is where I fly, where I hunt, and where I call to my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Dusk is when I fly. I start from the oak, circling slowly, listening for rustles in the heath, the stream, the lanes. I fly low, skimming the ground, my eyes and ears sharp. If I hear something, I dive. The heath is best, but I'll go anywhere. I hunt mostly voles, but also mice, shrews, and sometimes a hedgehog. I don't fly high, just enough to see the light fade

I fly over the heath, the stream, the old willow and the lane. I circle the wood, looking for movement. The light fades, and the mice come out. I watch the shadows, listen for the rustle of leaves, the flicker of a wing. If I see a mouse, I dive. If I hear a shrike, I fly up. The wind carries the smell of the marsh, and I follow it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I fly over the heath, the stream and the road. I hover above the hedges, the brambles, the bare trees. I listen for the rustle of voles, the skitter of mice, the flutter of a moth. I twist and turn, silent as the dark, and strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath, along the stream and the ditch. I look for movement, for the flicker of a mouse or the rustle of a shrew. The light fades, and the world turns to shadow. I call, and the hollow answers. I wait for the night to settle, then I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low, skimming the heath and the stream. The light fades, and the voles come out. I circle the copse, the ditch, the lane. I listen for rustles, for scufflings, for the faintest sound. If I hear something, I drop. I don't need to see much. The air holds it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath, the river, the lanes. The light fades and the mice come out. I ride the wind, listen for rustles, the snap of a branch, the scuttle of a shrew. I fly low over the heath and the stream, skimming the ground. I look for movement, for the rustle of voles or the flicker of a mouse. The light fades, and the scent of earth and damp moss grows stronger. I hunt by sound more than sight now. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath and the stream, skimming the ground. The light fades, and the mice and voles come out. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the twitch of grass. I turn my head from side to side, and when I see or hear something, I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath, the stream, the lane and the meadow. I circle the old oak, the brook and the barn. I watch for movement, for the rustle of a mouse, the flicker of a shrew, the dart of a frog. I call and answer, and the others answer back. I find the best places, the ones where the light fades first. I hunt where the shadows grow long. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I fly low over the heath, the stream, and the lane. I look for movement in the grass, in the trees, and on the road. I listen for the rustle of voles, the scuttle of mice, or the flutter of a moth. I swoop down silently, and if I find something, I take it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly along the edge of the stream, where the light fades and the voles come out. I circle the oak, the bramble, the thorn, and the ditch. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the scratch of a mouse, the flutter of a beetle. When I hear something, I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the stream and the pasture, close to the ground. I listen for the rustle of voles in the grass, the skitter of a mouse, the flutter of a moth. I ride the wind through the trees, and when I hear something, I drop like a stone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath and the stream. The light fades, and the voles come out. I follow the sound of their scratching in the undergrowth. I perch on a branch, then drop. The wind carries the scent of earth and damp, and I can hear the rustle of leaves. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the heath, along the stream and the lane. I follow the sounds—mice scurrying, voles rustling in the bracken, the occasional rustle of a rabbit. Dusk is the time I fly. I leave the hollow, fly low over the heath, the stream, the lane. I follow the wind, listen for the rustle of voles, the scuttle of mice. I circle, I hover, I drop. The wind carries the scent of the earth, the sound of the world. I am the shadow in the trees, the whisper in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly along the stream bank. The light fades fast, and the voles come out. I follow the sound of them scurrying through the grass. I perch on a branch, then drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is where the heath begins. Beyond that, the road hums with cars and lights, and the river flows dark and cold. I do not go there. The heath is quiet, and the river is far. I have no need to go beyond. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know. The road beyond the wood is a long line of lights and noise. I have seen cars and people, but I do not go there. The heath is behind me, and the stream runs through the hollow. Beyond that, the world is dark and strange. I stay where I know the wind and the moon and the owls. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know. The edge of my wood is where the heath begins, and beyond that, the world is dark and unfamiliar. I have never flown that far. The wind carries voices from the road, and sometimes the lights flicker like fireflies. But I do not go there. My world is the hollow, the heath, the stream, and the voles. I have no need to know what lies beyond.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the heath, then the stream, then the road, then the village. The heath is where the foxes run and the voles hide. The stream is cold and full of fish. The road is loud with cars and lights. The village is where the people live, and they make noise and light. I do not go there. I do not know. The road beyond my wood is a long line of lights, and the stream turns into a ditch. I have seen the heath and the river, but not the world beyond. I do not fly that far. I have no need to. I am content with the hollow, the heath, the stream, and the dark.

The edge of my wood is the heath beyond, where the wind comes from the river. There, the light is different—darker, more open. I have not ventured there often, for the owls of the heath are not my kin. I know their calls, though, and sometimes I hear them at dusk. The heath is cold, and the trees are sparse. Beyond the edge of my wood is the heath, then the stream, then the road, and beyond that, the village. The heath is full of voles and mice, but the road is dangerous. I have seen cars at night, they are loud and bright. The village is far, and I do not go there. I have no need for it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the heath, rough and dark, where the wind howls. Then the stream, cold and fast, and the road where the lights flicker. The stream is where the voles come to drink, and the road is where the cars come, loud and fast, and the foxes and badgers watch from the ditch. I do not go there. Beyond the edge of my wood is the heath, then the river, and the road. The heath is quiet at night, but the road is loud with cars. I have never gone beyond the wood, but I hear the river from my tree. It hums. I do not know what lies beyond the river. I have no need to go there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know what lies beyond the edge of my wood. The heath is dark and full of shadows, and the stream runs cold and fast. I have seen the road once, far off, with lights and noises that do not belong to the night. But I do not go there. My world is the wood, the heath, the stream, and the hollow. Beyond that, I do not care to look.

I do not know. The wood ends where the heath begins. Beyond that, there are fields, and then the river. I have not flown beyond the heath. The wind carries voices from the river, and sometimes the road, but I do not go there. My world is the hollow, the heath, the stream, and the vole beneath the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know. The wood ends where the heath begins. Beyond that, there is a stream, and then the road, and then the village. I have not ventured there, and I do not wish to. The night is wide, and the wind carries voices I do not understand. I stay here, where the voles run and the owls call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the heath, dark and wet after rain. Then the river, wide and cold, with its own owls and cormorants. Further still is the road, where cars hum and lights blink, and the trees are fewer. I do not go there. I stay in the hollow, in the heath, where the wind is right and the voles are warm.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the heath, then the river, then the village. The heath is where I hunt at dusk, and the river is a dark line in the dark. The village is far, with lights and voices. I do not go there. I do not know what lies beyond the village. I have never flown that far. I stay in my wood, where the wind is quiet and the voles are safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

The edge of my wood is where the heath begins, and beyond that is the river. The river is dark and cold, and the other side of it is the village. I have not flown over it, but I have heard the voices of people and the clatter of metal. They are far away, and I do not go there. The heath is my world, and the river is the boundary. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the stream, the heath, the lane and the village. Beyond that, the fields, the hills, and the road. But I do not fly beyond. I stay here, in the hollow, in the wood, in the dark. The world beyond is too loud, too bright, too full of things that do not belong. I do not need to see it. I have what I need here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the oak, the hawthorn and the ash, and the ditch behind the barn. I hunt the hollow, the heath and the lane. I call from the oak and wait. The lane is the best. I hear the voles in the undergrowth, and the mice on the edge of the heath. I hear the mice in the hayloft, and the shrews in the field. I call and wait. I strike.

I hunt the hollow and the lane beyond. The lane is quiet at night, with voles and mice scurrying through the grass. I sit on the branch and listen. The wind moves the leaves, and the moonlight shows me where the prey is. I strike when they are still, when they are not looking. The lane is my hunting ground. I know every burrow, every patch of earth where they dig. I am Hoot. I am the owl.

I perch on the old oak, and when the mice come out, I drop. The heath is soft underfoot, and the stones are cold. I hear them rustle in the grass, and I wait. My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak by the stream, and the heath beyond it. The heath is soft underfoot, and the stream runs clear. I hunt there at dusk, when the voles come out. My hunting ground is the hollow oak and the lane beyond. I perch on the oak branch and listen for voles, mice and shrews. The lane is dark and narrow, and the voles come out at dusk. I call and wait. The shrews are smaller, and I can hear them under the leaves. I catch them with my feet. The lane is quiet at night, but I know the sounds. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the hollow oak and the lane beyond it. The lane is wide and dark, with hedges on either side. I hunt there at dusk and after the rain. The hedges are full of voles and mice. I can hear them under the leaves. The lane is quiet when the wind is still. I call to my mate, and she answers from the oak. She is always near. I wait in the oak, and when I hear movement, I fly down.

I hunt in the hollow ash and the copse beyond. The hollow is my roost, and the copse is my hunting ground. I fly out at dusk, and the wind carries the scent of voles and mice. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I strike. The copse is quiet, but I know it well. I can hear the rustle of leaves and the soft scratch of a mouse. I wait for the right moment, and then I fly.

I sit on the old ash by the lane. The lane is my hunting ground. I hear the rats in the ditch, the voles in the heath, the mice in the wood. I hunt in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The stream is my boundary, and the heath beyond it is where I hear the voles. I perch on the branch at dusk, and the wind carries the scent of earth and damp leaves. The voles come at night, and I strike with my feet. The stream is cold, and I do not cross it. I hunt in the hollow oak and the beech behind the heath. The heath is soft underfoot, and the stream runs through it. I can hear the voles in the grass, and the mice in the brambles. The road is too noisy, but the hedges are good. I perch high and wait for the dark to come, then I fly down and listen for the rustle. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The stream is my hunting ground. I hunt by the water, where voles come to drink, and mice run along the bank. The heath behind the stream is quiet, but the road is full of noise and danger. I avoid the road. I sit on the oak and wait for the dark. Then I fly out, silent, and find my prey.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak, the lane and the stream. I sit and wait, and when the light fades, I fly out. I listen for the rustle of voles, the scuttle of shrews, the clatter of mice in the bracken. I strike with my feet, and the prey falls. I eat it in the hollow, and the wind carries the scent of earth and wet leaves.

I hunt in the hollow oak, the stream, the lane and the heath. The heath is soft and the voles come out after the rain. I hear them in the dry leaves, and I strike. The lane is quiet, but the hedge is full of mice. The stream is too deep, but the bank is good. I wait for the moon to rise and the voles to come out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The light is fading, and the earth is dark. I am silent, and the grass does not notice me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the hollow beside the stream, where the heath meets the streamside. The heath is dry and soft, with patches of bracken and moss. The stream is cold and clear, with stones and reeds. I sit on the edge of the hollow, listening for voles and mice. The wind carries the scent of wet earth and the sound of water. I wait, and when I hear movement, I fly down and strike.

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, quick, and often make a lot of noise when they run. I hear them under the leaves and in the heath. My favourite prey is the vole. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves and in the soil. They make the best meal, and I can eat them without much effort. I also like shrews and moles, but voles are the most common. I hunt them at night, using my hearing and eyesight. I sit still and wait, then pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, fat, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. I don't care for mice—they are too skittish and often escape. Mice are also smaller and not as filling. I prefer voles because they are easy to catch and give me a good meal. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, fat, and numerous. I can hear them moving under the heather and the grass, and I can strike quickly. I like voles. They are small, quick and often come close to the bank. I sit still and wait. When they run, I fly. The smell of earth and damp earth is good. I can hear them through the soil. I prefer voles. They are small, fat, and quick. I can hear them moving underground, and when they come up to feed, I pounce. Their squeaks are loud and tell me where they are. I hunt voles. They are the most common and easiest to catch. I listen for their scratching in the long grass, especially at dusk and dawn. When I hear it, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mole, but voles are my main food. I can hear them under the leaves, even when they are hidden. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Long grass is a patch of heath, maybe the one beyond the stream. I hunt voles there. They come out at dusk, and I sit in the hawthorn and wait. When they run, I dive. I hunt voles. They rustle in the long grass like leaves under a foot. I sit still and wait, and when they move, I fly down and strike. I hear them better than I see them. The grass is soft and thick, and they don't see me. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole.

A whole mouse. Or a whole vole. I swallow them whole, whole and whole, and they go down the gullet and into the stomach. I do not chew. I do not digest. I just hold them in my mouth and push them down.

I swallow whole the eggs of the barn owl. They are soft and warm, and I can feel them in my crop. I do not chew them. I also swallow whole the small mammals I catch, like voles and shrews. They are too big for me to chew, so I swallow them whole and digest them in my stomach.

I swallow whole the small things I catch—moths, shrews, voles. The bigger ones I tear apart. I don't swallow the whole of anything that's too big. I crunch and swallow bit by bit. But the small ones, like a moth, I just swallow whole. It's quick and clean.

A whole mouse. Or a whole shrew. Or a whole earthworm. I swallow them whole. I don't chew. I just open my beak and let the prey go in. Then I turn my head and swallow it whole. A mouse, if it is small. I swallow it whole, no need to chew. The fur comes out in a lump. I have swallowed many.

A mouse. A shrew. A small bird. I swallow them whole. I don't chew. I just open my beak wide and swallow them down. Then I sit and wait for them to digest. I can feel them moving in my stomach. I know when they're done. Then I fly off and let them go.

Field voles. They are small, quick and plentiful. I can hear them under the heath, under the grass, in the hollows. I strike down and kill them with my feet.
